title: A Website Is a Conversation
description: Understand the web as an exchange: a browser asks for a resource, a web service sends something back, and the browser uses what it receives.

objectives.statement: Understand the web as an exchange: a browser asks for a resource, a web service sends something back, and the browser uses what it receives.

content.title: Start here
content.hook: You type an address into a browser. A moment later, something appears on the screen.
content.context:
It feels like the page simply appeared. It did not.

A useful first model is:

**You ask. The web answers. The browser uses the answer.**

That is enough for now. You do not need protocol details yet.

content.question:
You open `https://example.com` and something appears.

Which statement best describes what happened?

options.text: The browser already contained the page, so it simply revealed it.
The browser asked for something and received information it could use.
The web service reached into your computer and drew the page directly.
The operating system invented the page after the browser asked for it.

feedback.correct: Right. The useful model is ask → receive → use. The browser is not simply revealing a page that was already sitting on the screen.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The useful model is ask → receive → use. The browser is not simply revealing a page that was already sitting on the screen.

content.title: The exchange
content.text:
A **request** is a message asking for a resource or action.

A **response** is what comes back.

A response might contain a page, an image, data, or an error. The important idea is the exchange itself.

For now, picture this:

```text
Browser  →  request  →  web service
Browser  ←  response ←  web service
```

One visit can involve more than one request. We will come back to that later.

content.question:
You ask for a resource. The web service sends back an error saying the resource was not found.

What does that tell you?

options.text: A response came back, but it reported a problem.

feedback.correct: Right. An error is still a response. The exchange happened; the result just was not the result you wanted.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. An error is still a response. The exchange happened; the result just was not the result you wanted.

content.question:
Suppose one requested resource arrives successfully, but another requested resource returns an error.

What is the best prediction?

options.text: Every other request must fail too.
The browser can still use the successful resource, while the failed resource may affect part of the final result.
The browser can no longer receive responses.

feedback.correct: Right. Requests can succeed or fail independently. A single failed resource changes what the browser has available to work with.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Requests can succeed or fail independently. A single failed resource changes what the browser has available to work with.

content.prompt:
Say it in your own words. Complete this sentence without using the words “request” or “response”:

“When a browser gets something from the web, it first ________, then it ________, and then it ________.”
content.sampleResponse: asks for information, receives information, and uses that information.

content.question:
A developer says:

> “A website is just a file sitting somewhere on the web. The browser downloads it, and that is basically the whole story.”

What is missing?

options.text: The exchange between the browser and the web service, plus the fact that a page can involve multiple resources.
The name of the developer who built the page.

feedback.correct: Right. The file metaphor is incomplete. A web page is part of an exchange, and the browser can need additional resources to produce the final result.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The file metaphor is incomplete. A web page is part of an exchange, and the browser can need additional resources to produce the final result.

content.title: Forge takeaway
takeaways: Mental model: The web is an exchange of information. A browser asks for something, receives a response, and uses that response to do work.
Senior habit: When something goes wrong, ask: What was requested? What came back?
